sections.h2: What is Brantley County, Georgia, like?
sections.html:
Brantley County is a rural county in southeast Georgia with its seat at Nahunta. It spreads over roughly 442 square miles of dry ground, with the Satilla River running through it, according to Wikipedia. Georgia voters approved the county's creation on November 2, 1920, carving it from parts of Charlton, Pierce and Wayne counties.

Census QuickFacts shows 18,021 residents in 2020 and about 18,936 by mid-2025. It also reports 8,537 housing units, homes worth a median $99,600 and 79.9 percent owner occupancy over the 2020 to 2024 survey period (Census QuickFacts). Just 77 building permits were issued in 2025, which tells you new construction is thin. Most sellers are longtime owners of a single-family house, a tract of land or a mobile home.

sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Brantley County?
sections.html:
The Brantley County Government Annex, 10405 Main Street North in Nahunta, houses both offices. One sends and collects the bills, and the other decides what each parcel is worth. The rate itself is set by elected boards, so neither office can lower it.

The county's tax offices page lists both numbers, and the commissioner's own site at brantleytax.com and the assessor's site at qpublic.net give the details below.

sections.h2: What does the Brantley County tax commissioner bill?
sections.html:
According to its website, the commissioner's office is responsible for ad valorem tax on these kinds of property:

  • Real property, meaning land and buildings
  • Personal property
  • Motor vehicles
  • Mobile homes
  • Timber

You can search any parcel and pay online through the same site. The site's news page carries tax sale notices, a list of excess funds and the office's holiday closings. Look there before you list a home with unpaid years on it, since a parcel headed to tax sale is a hard sell.

The due date for the annual bill is printed on the bill itself. If yours is missing, phone 912-462-5723 and request both the due date and the amount needed to clear the account.

Keep a printout of the paid receipt for every year you own the property. Whoever handles the closing will want to see that earlier years are clear, and a receipt from the commissioner answers that at once.

sections.h2: How are homes valued in Brantley County?
sections.html:
The assessor's website reports that every schedule was updated in 2025 along with a full re-evaluation of all properties. The office keeps files on 13,406 real property parcels, 602 personal property accounts and 2,346 mobile homes without a homestead exemption.

Assessed value in Georgia is 40 percent of what a property was worth on January 1. Returns are taken from January 1 until April 1, per the assessor's site. An owner who files no return gets an assessment notice in mid-May, and that notice starts the appeal clock.

  • Submit a return before April 1 if you want to declare your own value.
  • Open the notice as soon as it arrives and note the date it carries.
  • Phone the assessor at 912-462-5251 with any questions while time remains.

Because the re-evaluation changed values across the county, a home that looked cheap on paper a few years ago may now carry a noticeably different assessment. Pull the current record before you set a sale price.

Before listing, compare the county's record of your house with what is really there. Wrong square footage, a shed that was torn down or an addition that was never recorded are easier to fix before a buyer's appraiser spots them.

sections.h2: What is the process for challenging a Brantley County assessment?
sections.html:
The assessment notice opens a 45-day window, and the assessor's site warns that you get only that one. A challenge starts with the Board of Tax Assessors. Georgia's usual path then moves to the Board of Equalization and last to Superior Court, and arbitration is offered in place of the board hearing.

Grounds are value, uniformity and taxability. Complaints about the size of the bill do not count, since the bill follows the millage rate, which cannot be appealed.

  • Write the appeal out and keep your own copy.
  • Collect recent nearby sales and any repair quotes.
  • Ask the assessor how a hearing is requested.

The count runs from the notice date, so a mailbox you rarely check can cost you days.

sections.h2: What do the local housing numbers say to a Brantley County seller?
sections.html:
Brantley is thinly settled: density was 40.7 per square mile in the 2020 count, and 99.3 percent of residents lived in rural areas. Buyers tend to be local, and many properties are big lots or mobile home sites. QuickFacts lists 6,599 households, and 94.3 percent of residents had not moved in the past year, so listings are scarce and owners stay put (Census QuickFacts).

Median gross rent is $755, and a mortgaged owner spends a median $1,087 monthly; both are the lowest figures among the four counties compared. Three practical points follow for anyone weighing a sale:

  • Family and inherited land is common, so check whose names appear on the deed and on the tax bill before you list.
  • Brantley is part of the Brunswick metropolitan area, and Wayne, Glynn, Camden, Charlton, Ware and Pierce counties touch it, so buyers often shop those neighbors too.
  • Nearly 19 percent of residents are 65 or older (19.1 percent in QuickFacts), so estate and heir questions come up often. After an owner's death, ask the probate court how to proceed.

sections.h2: What should a Brantley County seller do about tax owed at closing?
sections.html:
Begin by getting a payoff amount from the tax commissioner, because unpaid county taxes must be cleared before a buyer can receive clean title. Then have the settlement agent work out each side's share of the year's bill.

If the house is a mobile home, confirm whether it is billed on its own or together with the land, since the assessor tracks non-homesteaded mobile homes as separate accounts. Homestead status affects this, so ask the assessor which treatment your home has.

Owners hurt by the Highway 82 fire can call the county commissioners' office at 912-462-5256, extension 5, about the recovery resources on the county website. Ask the assessor how fire damage is reflected in your record before you price the property.

faqs.q: How can I pay my Brantley County tax bill?
faqs.a: Pay the tax commissioner, either online at brantleytax.com or in person at Suite D of the Government Annex, 10405 Main Street North, Nahunta. The office number is 912-462-5723, and it posts weekday hours of 8:00 to 4:30.

faqs.q: What is the appeal deadline for a Brantley County assessment?
faqs.a: The deadline is 45 days after the date printed on the notice. The assessor's website treats that window as firm, so file in writing before it ends.

faqs.q: Does the Brantley County assessor set my tax bill?
faqs.a: No. The assessor sets the value only. The county commissioners and the school board set millage rates, and the tax commissioner sends the bill.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Brantley County house if taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the back taxes are paid at or before closing so the buyer gets clear title. Request a payoff from the tax commissioner and make sure it appears on the settlement statement.

faqs.q: When are Brantley County property tax returns due?
faqs.a: Returns are taken from January 1 until April 1 each year. Owners who miss that cutoff receive assessment notices in mid-May, and the 45-day appeal period starts then.
